current_note: TICK 22:22. E01 mid-build (plan written, 991 lines; build in flight). Driver did independent work rather than idling and produced a SECOND-OPINION top-20 from the vault lane under the Court's own floors, saved to .agents/plans/e01-driver-reference-top20.md so the builder's output can be compared rather than accepted. POSITIVE SIGNAL: the independent list contains simonw (Simon Willison), obra (Jesse Vincent) and akitaonrails (Fabio Akita) - the vault lane genuinely finds real, well-known engineers. TWO FALSE-POSITIVE FIXTURES CAPTURED, and they matter more than the pass. The driver flagged koala73 and mvanhorn as automation on shape alone, checked them, and WAS WRONG. koala73 shows 24 repos / 23 not-owned / 1 distinct basename - the textbook fork-farm fingerprint - but is Elie Habib, 4,099 followers, account since 2011, and the 23 not-owned repos are FORKS OF HIS OWN PROJECT (926 pushes to koala73/worldmonitor). A popular repo with forks is indistinguishable from a fork farm by that shape. mvanhorn shows 204 repos / 200 basenames / 4 not-owned - the Dicklesworthstone mass-self-repo fingerprint, and it sits UNDER the 15/day rate flag at 8.84 - but is Matt Van Horn, 4,901 followers, since 2010, pushing to real differently-named projects. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE EPIC: shape heuristics produce false positives on genuinely prolific developers, which is the Court's stated biggest risk instantiated on the very first list. Account context (followers, account age, whether the dominant repo is the person's own substantive project) is what actually separated these cases, and that costs one GitHub API call per candidate which the design must budget. This is the strongest argument yet for the Court's flag-for-review-never-auto-exclude ruling: an automatic shape exclusion would have dropped a 4,099-follower maintainer and a 15-year veteran on day one. Both are now regression fixtures the epic must not exclude.
